_: Department drawings mapped to LEARN note sections. (1) Line drawings from the owner's uploads CERVICAL FASCIA.pdf and GREAT VESSELS OF THE NECK.pdf and the CNS-levels scans: prepare.py crops them (embedded images, or a y-band of a scanned page). (2) Figures of the Kasr Al Ainy NEU 205 book (205_NEU_Published.pdf, as the owner's 'Labeled Drawings and Pictures' Part PDFs; entries with 'book' = its figure number): prepare_book.py extracts them, including the book's colour plates, since they are part of the official book. Book figures that repeat a drawing already here keep one copy, the sharper; figures left out are listed in docs/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md. Captions are ours, from the labels on each figure. Both scripts write plain JPEGs into one folder outside the repo; encrypt.mjs writes the encrypted copies to source/public/dept/ and the manifest to source/public/dept-figs-v16-data.js.

figs.ans: Department answers: 1 comma tract (completes reflex arcs) · 2 substantia gelatinosa of Rolando (2nd-order pain & temperature) · 3 dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clark's nucleus) · 4 ventral spinothalamic tract (from the main sensory nucleus) · 5 rubrospinal tract (ventral tegmental decussation)

figs.cap: CNS level 2 · Spinal cord (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 comma tract (descending fibres from the cuneate tract) · 2 main sensory nucleus (gives the ventral spinothalamic tract) · 3 lateral spinothalamic tract (continues as the spinal lemniscus) · 4 reticulospinal tract · 5 lateral corticospinal tract (voluntary movement)

figs.cap: CNS level 3 · Spinal cord (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 Lissauer's tract (1st-order pain & temperature) · 2 lateral vestibulospinal tract · 3 sulcomarginal tract (continuation of the MLB) · 4 ventral spinocerebellar tract (both sides of the lower limb) · 5 Clark's nucleus (same side)

figs.cap: CNS level 4 · Spinal cord (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 reticulospinal tract · 2 lateral corticospinal tract · 3 septomarginal (oval) tract (completes reflex arcs) · 4 main sensory nucleus (2nd-order crude touch) · 5 lateral spinothalamic tract (2nd-order pain & temperature)

figs.cap: CNS level 5 · Medulla, motor decussation (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 gracile nucleus (2nd-order proprioception to the cortex) · 2 dorsal spinocerebellar tract (to a subcortical level) · 3 medial longitudinal bundle (continues as the sulcomarginal tract) · 4 rubrospinal tract · 5 pyramidal fibres (upper two-thirds of area 4) crossing in the motor decussation

figs.cap: CNS level 6 · Medulla, sensory decussation (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 internal arcuate fibres (sensory decussation) · 2 spinal nucleus of the trigeminal (axons join the trigeminal lemniscus) · 3 dorsal spinocerebellar tract · 4 medial lemniscus (2nd-order fine touch) · 5 hypoglossal nucleus

figs.cap: CNS level 7 · Pons (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 trigeminal lemniscus (ends in VPMN) · 2 medial lemniscus (ends in VPLN) · 3 medial longitudinal bundle (continues as the sulcomarginal tract) · 4 the bundle keyed as continuing as the septomarginal tract · 5 transverse pontine fibres (separate the pyramidal bundles)

figs.cap: CNS level 8 · Midbrain, inferior colliculus (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles · 2 trochlear nucleus · 3 inferior colliculus (auditory reflexes) · 4 lateral lemniscus · 5 crus cerebri: pyramidal fibres from the upper two-thirds of area 4

figs.cap: CNS level 9 · Midbrain, superior colliculus (department histology drawing)
figs.ans: Department answers: 1 dorsal tegmental decussation (tectospinal tracts) · 2 red nucleus · 3 oculomotor nucleus · 4 superior colliculus (visual reflexes) · 5 medial lemniscus

The tympanic membrane: pars flaccida and tensa, malleolar folds, handle of malleus, umbo, cone of light

The middle ear as a box: roof (tegmen tympani), floor (jugular bulb), anterior wall (carotid canal, auditory tube), posterior wall (aditus, pyramid), medial wall (promontory, oval and round windows, facial canal)
Walls of the middle ear in section: tegmen tympani, mastoid antrum and aditus, facial canal, auditory tube, carotid canal, tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve
The middle ear in colour: tympanic membrane, malleus, incus and stapes, and the pharyngotympanic tube
The ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) and the muscles of the middle ear: tensor tympani and stapedius
The inner ear: semicircular canals and ducts, utricle, saccule, cochlea with scala vestibuli, cochlear duct and scala tympani
The membranous labyrinth: cochlear duct, saccule, utricle, semicircular ducts, endolymphatic duct and sac, with the maculae
The vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII): cochlear and vestibular parts from the inner ear through the internal acoustic meatus to the brain stem
Lymph nodes of the head and neck: superficial ring (occipital, mastoid, parotid, facial, submandibular, submental) and the deep cervical chain
Veins and lymph of the thyroid gland: superior, middle and inferior thyroid veins; prelaryngeal, pretracheal and deep cervical nodes
The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and its arch for the vertebral artery and the first cervical nerve
Atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints from behind: membrana tectoria, apical and alar ligaments, capsules
The embryo at the pharyngeal arch stage: arches, clefts, otic and lens placodes, heart bulge
Nerves of the pharyngeal arches: trigeminal (1st), facial (2nd), glossopharyngeal (3rd) and vagus (4th and 6th)
Cartilages of the pharyngeal arches and what they become: Meckel's (malleus, incus), Reichert's (stapes, styloid, hyoid), 3rd, 4th and 6th (hyoid, laryngeal cartilages)
The parts of each pharyngeal arch: cartilage, aortic arch, nerve, muscle, with the pouch inside and the cleft outside
The pharyngeal pouches and clefts and what each pouch becomes: tympanic cavity and auditory tube, palatine tonsil, parathyroids and thymus, ultimobranchial body
Pouch derivatives migrating: inferior parathyroid and thymus from the 3rd pouch, superior parathyroid from the 4th, ultimobranchial body, and the thyroid from the foramen caecum
Branchial anomalies: external branchial fistula, lateral cervical cyst, internal fistula into the tonsil, and where they lie along the sternomastoid
Development of the face (1): frontonasal, maxillary and mandibular processes around the stomodeum, nasal placodes and pits
Development of the face (2): medial and lateral nasal prominences, the intermaxillary segment, and where a cleft lip forms
Development of the palate (1): palatine shelves beside the tongue, then fused shelves with the nasal septum, incisive foramen
Development of the palate (2): palatine shelves rising above the tongue to meet the primary palate and the nasal septum
Cleft lip and cleft palate in infants: unilateral and bilateral cleft lip, cleft palate, oblique facial cleft
Types of cleft of the lip and palate relative to the incisive foramen: anterior, posterior and complete clefts
Bifid tongue: a developmental anomaly of the tongue
Tongue tie (ankyloglossia): a short frenulum linguae
Macroglossia: an abnormally large tongue
Microglossia: an abnormally small tongue

Development of the tongue: lateral lingual swellings and tuberculum impar (1st arch) form the body, the copula and hypobranchial eminence (3rd and 4th arches) form the root, with the foramen caecum between
Chemical synapse (vesicles, neurotransmitter, ionotropic and metabotropic receptors) compared with an electrical synapse (gap junction channels)
Structure of a chemical synapse: presynaptic knob with vesicles and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, synaptic cleft, receptors on the postsynaptic neuron
Ionotropic receptor (the transmitter opens a channel) and metabotropic receptor (the transmitter acts through a G protein and adenyl cyclase)
Steps of chemical transmission: action potential, Ca2+ entry, vesicle docking and release, transmitter binding, graded postsynaptic potential
IPSP: activation of an inhibitory synapse moves the membrane away from threshold (hyperpolarisation)
EPSP: activation of an excitatory synapse gives a small depolarisation below threshold
Summation: three synapses firing together (spatial, top) or one synapse firing repeatedly (temporal, bottom) bring the neuron to threshold
Presynaptic facilitation (serotonin neuron) and presynaptic inhibition (GABA neuron) acting on the terminal of the presynaptic cell
Presynaptic facilitation and inhibition through an axoaxonic synapse: one neuron changes the effect of another on a third

LTP and LTD at a glutamate synapse: high-frequency stimulation gives a large Ca2+ surge through NMDA receptors, CaMKII and more AMPA receptors; low frequency gives a small surge, phosphatases and fewer AMPA receptors
Types of inhibition by inhibitory interneurons: lateral inhibition, recurrent (Renshaw) inhibition of the motor neuron, and reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist
Neuronal pools: divergence, convergence and the excitation field (discharge and facilitated zones)
Neuronal circuits: facilitation and inhibition within a pool, input to output
A parallel after-discharge circuit: the input reaches the output neuron through chains of different lengths, prolonging the output
The sensory unit, its receptive field and the labelled line to the brain
Receptor potential in a Pacinian corpuscle: the deformed area depolarises and local current fires an action potential at the first node of Ranvier
Generator potential amplitude rises with stimulus strength, steeply at first and then levelling off
A larger generator potential above threshold fires action potentials at a higher frequency

Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway: first-order neurons in the gracile and cuneate fasciculi, second-order in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, third-order in the thalamus to the somatosensory cortex
The trigeminal sensory pathway: V1, V2 and V3 through the trigeminal ganglion to the brain stem nuclei, thalamus and somatosensory cortex
The lateral (temperature and pain) and anterior (crude touch and pressure) spinothalamic tracts, with first-, second- and third-order neurons
Somatosensory areas I and II and the body map on area I
The sensory homunculus on the postcentral gyrus: large areas for the face, lips and hand
Discharge of cold-pain, cold, warmth and heat-pain receptors across skin temperature
Chemistry of pain at a wound: bradykinin, prostaglandins, K+, histamine from mast cells, and substance P released back from the nerve ending
Primary and secondary hyperalgesia and allodynia: sensitised nociceptors in the injured area and touch fibres driving pain neurons around it
Herpes zoster: the virus in a dorsal root ganglion gives pain and a rash along one dermatome
Referred pain: where pain from the heart, liver and gallbladder, stomach, appendix, kidney and ureter, bladder and other organs is felt on the body surface
Why visceral pain is referred: the convergence theory and the facilitation theory
The analgesia system (periaqueductal grey, raphe magnus, enkephalin neurons) and gate control in the substantia gelatinosa
Brown-Séquard syndrome: lost fine touch, vibration and position sense on the side of the lesion, lost pain and temperature on the opposite side, complete loss at the level
Motor control: motor cortex (upper motor neuron), basal ganglia, cerebellum and reticular formation acting on the alpha and gamma motor neurons and the muscle spindle
The stretch reflex: muscle spindle, sensory nerve, motor nerve back to the same muscle
The reflex arc: receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron and effector
The muscle spindle: nuclear bag and nuclear chain fibres, primary (Ia) and secondary (II) endings, dynamic and static gamma efferents
Spindle discharge when the muscle is stretched, with more gamma discharge, with alpha discharge alone, and with alpha-gamma coactivation
The damping function of the stretch reflex: an 8-per-second signal gives a smooth contraction with the spindles intact (A) and a jerky one after the dorsal roots are cut (B)
Supraspinal centres that facilitate the gamma motor neurons: cerebral cortex, facilitatory reticular formation, cerebellum, vestibular nucleus
Supraspinal centres that inhibit the gamma motor neurons: area 4s, basal ganglia, palaeocerebellum and the ventromedial medullary reticular formation
Decerebrate rigidity: rigid extended legs, pointed toes, straight tense arms beside the body, flexed wrists and curled fingers
Withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes: the stimulated leg flexes to withdraw and the opposite leg extends to support
The Golgi tendon organ lies in series with the muscle and the muscle spindle in parallel, with their afferents and the alpha and gamma motor neurons
The reticular activating system: collaterals from sensory, visual and auditory pathways feed the reticular formation, which radiates to the whole cerebral cortex
The vestibular apparatus: semicircular canals with the crista in each ampulla, utricle and saccule with their maculae, type I and type II hair cells
The planes of the semicircular canals: anterior and posterior (vertical) and lateral (horizontal), on both sides
The crista ampullaris: hair cells with stereocilia and a kinocilium embedded in the gelatinous cupula
Morphological polarisation of vestibular hair cells: bending toward the kinocilium depolarises, bending away hyperpolarises
How a hair cell transduces: bending toward the kinocilium opens K+ channels (endolymph is high in K+), Ca2+ enters and transmitter is released; bending away closes them
Rotation and the horizontal canals: endolymph lag bends the cupulae, stimulating one side and inhibiting the other, and the reverse when rotation stops
Vestibular nuclei and their connections: medial longitudinal fasciculus to the eye muscle nuclei (III, IV, VI), lateral and medial vestibulospinal tracts, cerebellum, thalamus
Orientation of the maculae: hair cells of the utricle lie horizontal and those of the saccule vertical
The maculae and linear acceleration: the otolithic membrane lags on starting and runs on when stopping, bending the hair cells
Structure of the macula of the utricle and saccule: hair cells and supporting cells under the otolithic membrane with its otoliths
Upper motor neuron (motor cortex to the anterior horn) and lower motor neuron (anterior horn to the muscle)
Functional areas of the cerebral cortex: primary motor, premotor, primary sensory and association, visual, auditory, olfactory and gustatory areas
The motor homunculus on the primary motor cortex: large areas for the hand, face, tongue and larynx
Motor areas on the lateral surface: primary motor cortex with its body map, premotor and supplementary areas (hand skills, head rotation), frontal eye field, Broca's area
The corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts from the motor cortex through the midbrain, pons and medulla, the pyramidal decussation, and the lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts
The basal ganglia in the hemisphere: caudate nucleus and putamen (striatum), globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra
Output of the basal ganglia: neostriatum, globus pallidus, subthalamic nuclei and substantia nigra to the brain stem reticular formation and the rubrospinal, vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts
The direct and indirect pathways: cortex, neostriatum, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, thalamus, and dopamine from the substantia nigra
Parkinsonism: rigidity and tremor of the head and limbs, forward tilt of the trunk, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait with short steps
Basal ganglia circuits in normal, parkinsonism, hemiballismus and chorea: which link is lost and which pathway takes over
The cerebellar circuit: mossy fibres through granule cells and climbing fibres from the inferior olive to Purkinje cells, which inhibit the deep nuclei
Functional parts of the cerebellum: vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe), spinocerebellum and cerebrocerebellum, and what each controls
Afferent tracts to the cerebellum through its three peduncles: spinocerebellar, pontocerebellar, olivocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar
Efferent tracts from the cerebellum: dentate to the red nucleus and thalamus (cerebellothalamocortical), fastigial to the reticular formation and vestibular nuclei
The intermediate cerebellum compares intention with performance: motor cortex, spinocerebellar feedback, red nucleus and thalamus back to the cortex
Planning and executing a movement: association cortex, basal ganglia and lateral cerebellum plan; premotor and motor cortex with the intermediate cerebellum execute
The diencephalon in sagittal section: thalamus and interthalamic adhesion, hypothalamus (optic chiasma, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mamillary body), epithalamus (habenula, pineal body)
EEG waves: alpha, beta, theta and delta
Alpha block: alpha waves with the eyes closed are replaced by fast low-voltage waves when the eyes open
EEG through the stages of sleep: relaxed wakefulness (alpha), stage 1 (theta), stage 2 (sleep spindles and K-complexes), stages 3 and 4 (delta), and REM sleep
Language areas: Broca's area (word formation), Wernicke's area (language comprehension), the naming and visual processing of words, and the limbic association area
The three coats of the eye: outer (cornea and sclera), middle (choroid, ciliary body, iris) and inner (retina, its photosensitive and non-visual parts)
The eyeball in section: cornea, anterior and posterior chambers, iris, lens with the zonular fibres, ciliary body, vitreous, retina, choroid, sclera, fovea, optic nerve
Focal length: parallel rays converge through a convex lens to the focal point
A lens with sharply curved sides has a short focal length and one with gently curved sides a long one: the basis of accommodation
Aqueous drainage at the normal angle: from the posterior chamber through the pupil to the trabecular meshwork
Glaucoma: an open angle where fluid drains, and a closed angle where the iris blocks the trabecular meshwork and the canal of Schlemm
The corneal reflex: afferent through the ophthalmic division of V, efferent through the facial nuclei and nerve to orbicularis oculi on both sides
The iridocorneal angle: canal of Schlemm, spaces of Fontana, ciliary body and the suspensory ligament of the lens
The ciliary muscle (meridional and circular fibres) and the suspensory ligaments holding the lens
The pupillary light reflex: optic nerve to the pretectal area, Edinger-Westphal nucleus, oculomotor nerve and ciliary ganglion to the sphincter pupillae, on both sides
Myopia (light focused in front of the retina, corrected with a concave lens) and hypermetropia (behind the retina, corrected with a convex lens)
Spherical aberration: peripheral rays focus nearer the lens than central rays
Chromatic aberration: blue light focuses nearer the lens than yellow and red
